text:
PREMISE: Tax cuts at the top and cuts to food aid are separate fights.

STEP 1: CBO: the 2025 law gives the top 10% of households about $13,600 a year on average.
STEP 2: Lost revenue means more borrowing. Net interest hit $963 billion in ten months of fiscal 2026.
STEP 3: The same law cuts SNAP by about $186 billion over ten years.
STEP 4: Money flows up through tax cuts and comes back out of grocery budgets.

CONCLUSION: It's one fight. Follow a dollar from the tax cut to the food line.

PREMISE: Home insurance is a climate issue, not a poverty issue.

STEP 1: Storms and land loss drove insurers out of Louisiana after 2020 and 2021.
STEP 2: A standard homeowners policy cost about $5,400 in 2024, per the Climate and Community Institute.
STEP 3: Landlords pass insurance costs into rent. LSUS found 48.4% of Louisiana renters were cost-burdened in 2023.
STEP 4: Louisiana already has the nation's highest official poverty rate, 19.7%.

CONCLUSION: The storm hits the coast. The bill hits the poorest family's budget. Climate and poverty are the same story here.

PREMISE: Heat on the job is a weather problem.

STEP 1: The AFL-CIO estimates about 530 workers died from heat on the job in 2024.
STEP 2: There's still no final federal heat rule, and Louisiana has no state heat standard.
STEP 3: Seven states have their own rules. Louisiana, one of the hottest, doesn't.
STEP 4: Water, rest and shade are cheap. Leaving them optional is a choice.

CONCLUSION: Weather brings the heat. Labor law decides who dies of it.

PREMISE: Medicaid cuts mostly hit cities.

STEP 1: About 1.6 million Louisianans are on Medicaid.
STEP 2: Rural hospitals depend heavily on Medicaid patients. A Markey letter flagged 33 of Louisiana's 49 rural hospitals as at risk (estimate).
STEP 3: When a rural hospital closes, everyone in town loses the ER, insured or not.
STEP 4: Many of those towns are white, working-class and poor.

CONCLUSION: Medicaid cuts land hard on rural white towns too. That's common ground, not a city-versus-country fight.

PREMISE: A $7.25 wage is a private deal between a boss and a worker.

STEP 1: Full time at $7.25 is $15,080 a year.
STEP 2: Workers earning that often qualify for SNAP and Medicaid.
STEP 3: Public programs then fill the gap between the paycheck and survival.
STEP 4: The employer keeps the savings. The public covers the rest.

CONCLUSION: A poverty wage isn't private. Taxpayers pick up what the employer won't pay.

PREMISE: Union decline and billionaire wealth are unrelated trends.

STEP 1: Louisiana's union rate was 4.4% in 2025. Nationally, private-sector membership was 5.9%.
STEP 2: Workers' share of business income hit 52.8% in 2026, the lowest since BLS records began in 1947.
STEP 3: Fed data: the top 1% held about 31.6% of household wealth. The bottom half held about 2.5%.
STEP 4: When workers can't bargain, more of what they make flows to owners.

CONCLUSION: Weak unions and record wealth at the top are two ends of one rope.

PREMISE: Wage theft is a labor issue. Hunger is a poverty issue.

STEP 1: DOL recovered about $1,465 per worker in fiscal 2025 from employers who underpaid.
STEP 2: Average SNAP is about $188 a month per person.
STEP 3: So one worker's recovered pay averages almost eight months of a person's food aid.
STEP 4: Stolen wages push families onto the programs that are now being cut.

CONCLUSION: Enforce wage law and you fight hunger. Ignore it and the food line grows.

PREMISE: Louisiana's tax system is neutral. Everyone pays the same rates.

STEP 1: Louisiana leans on sales taxes, about 10.1% combined, among the highest in the country.
STEP 2: ITEP found the lowest-income 20% paid about 13.1% of income in state and local taxes; the top 1% paid about 6.5%.
STEP 3: The 2024 flat income tax mostly helped the top. ITEP estimated the top 1% got about $15,431 and the middle about $87 (estimate).
STEP 4: Same rates on paper. Very different bites in real life.

CONCLUSION: A tax that takes twice the share from the poor isn't neutral. It's part of why Louisiana stays poor.

PREMISE: Social Security's funding gap and elder poverty are separate questions.

STEP 1: Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of poverty in 2025, more than any other program.
STEP 2: The Trustees project full benefits until 2034, then about 81%.
STEP 3: Payroll tax stops at $184,500 in wages. Income above that pays nothing in.
STEP 4: Lifting the cap closes much of the gap. Cutting benefits pushes elders back into poverty.

CONCLUSION: The cap is a poverty policy. Scrap it and you protect grandparents.

PREMISE: The gender pay gap is about women's choices.

STEP 1: Child care for one child costs about 9% to 16% of median family income, DOL data show.
STEP 2: Only 49% of private workers had paid family leave in 2026.
STEP 3: Without care or leave, mothers cut hours or leave jobs. That's one driver of lower pay.
STEP 4: Women earned about 82 cents per man's dollar in weekly pay in spring 2026.

CONCLUSION: Choices are made inside a system. Fund child care and leave, and the 'choice' changes.
sources: DOL National Database of Childcare Prices

text:
PREMISE: Ida's deaths were nature's fault.

STEP 1: The wind and water were nature.
STEP 2: Louisiana counted 26 early Ida deaths. At least 10 came from heat and 6 from carbon monoxide after the power went out.
STEP 3: Those deaths came from the grid failing and families running generators to cope.
STEP 4: Grid hardening, backup power and cooling centers are policy choices.

CONCLUSION: The storm was natural. The death toll after it was shaped by choices.

PREMISE: LNG plants bring money to local schools.

STEP 1: Big industrial projects in Louisiana often get local property tax exemptions.
STEP 2: The Sierra Club estimated one Plaquemines LNG exemption at about $834 million, roughly $316 million of it school money (estimate).
STEP 3: Running a terminal often takes a few hundred workers, per the same report.
STEP 4: Fewer jobs than promised, less school money than expected.

CONCLUSION: Ask what the exemption costs the classroom before you count the ribbon cutting.

PREMISE: Immigration and climate are separate debates.

STEP 1: After Katrina, Laura and Ida, immigrant crews did much of the gutting and roofing.
STEP 2: Hispanic and Latino work deaths in Louisiana rose from 12 in 2023 to 22 in 2024.
STEP 3: Workers without papers can't easily report wage theft or unsafe sites.
STEP 4: As storms get worse, the rebuild workforce grows, and so does the risk.

CONCLUSION: Climate recovery runs on immigrant labor. Protect those workers and you protect the rebuild.

PREMISE: Child labor and child poverty are unrelated.

STEP 1: The Labor Department found 5,272 minors working illegally in fiscal 2025.
STEP 2: At least 13 states introduced bills to weaken child labor protections in 2026.
STEP 3: Kids in poor families face the most pressure to earn.
STEP 4: The 2021 child tax credit cut child poverty to a record low. When it expired, that pressure came back.

CONCLUSION: Fight child poverty and you fight child labor. Cash for families beats kids on night shifts.

PREMISE: Medical bills are a health issue, not a poverty issue.

STEP 1: Census found out-of-pocket medical costs pushed about 7.7 million people into poverty in 2025.
STEP 2: 26.7 million people were uninsured all of 2025.
STEP 3: Medical debt in America totals about $220 billion.
STEP 4: A hospital bill can turn a working family poor overnight.

CONCLUSION: Health care is anti-poverty policy. Cover people and fewer fall.

PREMISE: Corporate taxes and your paycheck have nothing to do with each other.

STEP 1: CBO: corporate income tax receipts fell 23% in the first ten months of fiscal 2026.
STEP 2: Individual income tax receipts rose 7%.
STEP 3: The government still has bills to pay. When companies pay less, workers carry more.
STEP 4: The 2017 corporate cut promised raises. Research found wages didn't come close.

CONCLUSION: Every dollar companies stop paying is a dollar someone else pays, or a service someone loses.

PREMISE: Inheritances are a family matter.

STEP 1: The estate tax exemption is $15 million per person, $30 million per couple.
STEP 2: Assets held until death get their gains wiped clean for heirs. That's stepped-up basis.
STEP 3: Borrow against assets, never sell, pass them on: gains are never taxed.
STEP 4: Fed data show the top 1% holding nearly a third of household wealth.

CONCLUSION: Tax rules built for dynasties turn today's inequality into tomorrow's aristocracy.

PREMISE: The dead zone is a Gulf problem, not a corporate problem.

STEP 1: Fertilizer runoff from up the Mississippi feeds the dead zone, about 4,400 square miles in 2025.
STEP 2: Shrimpers and fishers lose catch and income.
STEP 3: The runoff costs nothing to those who send it downriver.
STEP 4: One industry's free waste is another industry's lost paycheck.

CONCLUSION: Unpriced pollution moves money from Gulf workers to upstream agribusiness.

PREMISE: Opioid deaths are a personal failing in poor white towns.

STEP 1: West Virginia reporting found nearly 9 million hydrocodone pills shipped to one pharmacy in Kermit, a town of a few hundred people.
STEP 2: Distributors and makers profited from the flood. Purdue's owners faced billions in settlements.
STEP 3: Overdose deaths fell 26.2% in 2024 as treatment and naloxone spread.
STEP 4: Medicaid is a major payer for addiction treatment. Cutting it threatens that progress.

CONCLUSION: Profit flooded the towns. Public health is pulling them out. Don't cut the rope.

PREMISE: Work requirements make sure people on Medicaid have jobs.

STEP 1: BLS counts 4.5 million people stuck in part-time jobs who want full-time hours.
STEP 2: Low-wage jobs often have shifting schedules that don't hit a fixed hour count.
STEP 3: The new rules require 80 hours a month and more frequent paperwork.
STEP 4: In Arkansas in 2018, about 18,000 people lost coverage, many over reporting.

CONCLUSION: The problem isn't missing workers. It's unsteady jobs and paperwork traps.

PREMISE: Weakening the NLRB is a Washington power fight that doesn't touch paychecks.

STEP 1: The NLRB went 345 days without a quorum in 2025.
STEP 2: Workers fired for organizing waited longer for rulings.
STEP 3: Union members earned about $230 a week more than nonunion workers in 2025.
STEP 4: Slow enforcement makes organizing riskier, so fewer workers get that premium.

CONCLUSION: A broken referee shows up in your weekly pay.

PREMISE: FEMA prevention grants and your insurance bill are unrelated.

STEP 1: FEMA ended BRIC in April 2025. Louisiana had about $721 million in projects at stake.
STEP 2: Those projects were drainage, stronger power lines and flood protection.
STEP 3: Insurers price risk. Less protection means more risk.
STEP 4: A court ruled the termination unlawful, but money has been slow to move.

CONCLUSION: Cut prevention today, pay higher premiums tomorrow.

PREMISE: Black unemployment rising is a Black community issue.

STEP 1: Black unemployment hit 7.0% in September 2026, versus 4.2% overall.
STEP 2: Black workers are often first hit when the economy turns.
STEP 3: Overall unemployment was also at its highest since 2021.
STEP 4: Layoffs that start with one group rarely stop there.

CONCLUSION: The first ones hit are the early warning for everyone. Stand together before it spreads.

PREMISE: Health insurance costs are separate from wages.

STEP 1: Average family coverage through an employer costs about $27,000 a year.
STEP 2: Employers count that as part of what they spend on you.
STEP 3: Every dollar that goes to premiums is a dollar that can't go to raises.
STEP 4: Rising premiums are one reason paychecks have barely grown.

CONCLUSION: Health costs eat wages before you ever see them. Fixing health care is a raise.

PREMISE: Power bills and heat deaths are separate problems.

STEP 1: Electricity prices rose 3.8% over the year to August 2026.
STEP 2: Families behind on bills face shutoffs.
STEP 3: CDC counted 2,391 heat-related deaths in 2024, mostly older people.
STEP 4: In a Gulf summer, a shutoff can be deadly.

CONCLUSION: No shutoffs in a heat wave. Affordable power is public health.

PREMISE: Coastal restoration is an environmental program, not a jobs program.

STEP 1: Louisiana spent about $21.4 billion on coastal projects from 2005 to 2023.
STEP 2: About 27,483 coastal well sites were dry or abandoned by 2017. Fewer than about 50 were filled in.
STEP 3: Dredging, pipe and heavy equipment are skills oil workers already have.
STEP 4: The Master Plan runs 50 years.

CONCLUSION: Restoration is both. It's the bridge from drilling jobs to rebuilding jobs.

PREMISE: Retirement is a personal savings problem.

STEP 1: Only 48% of the lowest-paid quarter of private workers even had access to a retirement plan in 2026.
STEP 2: Workers 65 and older die on the job at 9.1 per 100,000, nearly three times the overall rate.
STEP 3: Social Security is the main income for many older workers who can't save.
STEP 4: No plan plus low pay means working until your body gives out.

CONCLUSION: Retirement is a labor issue. Bargain for plans and protect Social Security.

PREMISE: Paid sick days are a perk for workers.

STEP 1: Only 63% of the lowest-paid quarter of workers had paid sick leave in 2026.
STEP 2: Many of those workers cook, serve food and care for elders.
STEP 3: Without sick pay, they come in sick.
STEP 4: Illness then spreads to customers and patients.

CONCLUSION: Paid sick leave protects the public, not just the worker.

PREMISE: Nursing home safety is a health care issue only.

STEP 1: During Ida, about 800 nursing home residents were moved into one warehouse, and residents died after.
STEP 2: Research has tied private equity ownership of nursing homes to higher death rates.
STEP 3: Cutting staff and backup power raises profit and risk together.
STEP 4: Storms test whether a business planned for people or for margins.

CONCLUSION: Climate, health care and ownership meet in the nursing home. Inspect and enforce.

PREMISE: Insurance denials are a paperwork issue.

STEP 1: Medicare Advantage plans denied 3.2 million prior authorization requests. Most weren't appealed.
STEP 2: Of those appealed, 81.7% were overturned.
STEP 3: People who don't appeal pay out of pocket or skip care.
STEP 4: Medical debt then follows them into collections.

CONCLUSION: A wrongful denial becomes a debt, and a debt becomes poverty.

PREMISE: Young people can't buy homes because they spend too much.

STEP 1: Student debt totals about $1.65 trillion.
STEP 2: Workers' share of income is at a record low, and real wages barely moved in a year.
STEP 3: Homeownership for people under 35 was about 35.2% in mid-2026.
STEP 4: High debt plus flat pay means no down payment.

CONCLUSION: It's not lattes. It's debt, wages and prices.

PREMISE: Families leaving the coast are just moving.

STEP 1: Isle de Jean Charles lost about 98% of its land since 1955.
STEP 2: Moving one small community cost a $48 million federal grant.
STEP 3: Families who move inland face rents and insurance costs they didn't have before.
STEP 4: Without help, climate moves turn into housing crises.

CONCLUSION: Climate displacement is a housing issue. Plan for it with real support.

PREMISE: Food banks can handle the SNAP cuts.

STEP 1: 47.9 million people lived in food-insecure households in 2024.
STEP 2: CBO estimates about $186 billion in SNAP cuts over ten years.
STEP 3: That's roughly $18.6 billion a year on average.
STEP 4: Charity can't replace a program that size.

CONCLUSION: When public aid shrinks, private charity can't fill a hole that big.

PREMISE: We can't afford food aid because of the debt.

STEP 1: Net interest reached $963 billion in ten months of fiscal 2026.
STEP 2: The average yearly SNAP cut is about $18.6 billion.
STEP 3: Interest payments in about a week's worth of that period would cover a year of the cut.
STEP 4: Tax cuts at the top added to the borrowing that drives interest.

CONCLUSION: It's not about affordability. It's about who gets paid first: bondholders or hungry families.

PREMISE: Workers are passive. They just take what they're given.

STEP 1: Labor's share hit a record low in 2026.
STEP 2: Workers in major strikes rose to 306,800 in 2025, up 13%.
STEP 3: Health care workers made up about 40% of strikers, many over staffing.
STEP 4: When the squeeze gets tight, workers push back.

CONCLUSION: Rising strikes are the other end of a falling labor share. People notice when they're shortchanged.

PREMISE: Immigrants are why Louisiana is poor.

STEP 1: Test the link. Foreign-born workers are about 19% of the U.S. workforce.
STEP 2: Louisiana has a smaller immigrant share than many richer states.
STEP 3: Its poverty tracks low wages, a $7.25 floor, regressive taxes and storm costs.
STEP 4: The chain breaks at the first link.

CONCLUSION: Blaming immigrants doesn't fit the facts. Look at wages, taxes and who sets them.

PREMISE: Climate change is the only reason insurance costs exploded.

STEP 1: Storms clearly drive losses, and that's the biggest factor.
STEP 2: Litigation costs played a role. Louisiana passed reforms.
STEP 3: Insurer exits left less competition.
STEP 4: Premiums still climbed after the reforms.

CONCLUSION: Climate is the main driver, not the only one. Name all the causes and you'll win the argument.

PREMISE: Tariffs protect American workers' paychecks.

STEP 1: Customs duties brought in $154 billion in ten months of fiscal 2026.
STEP 2: Importers pay them and often pass costs to consumers.
STEP 3: Prices rose 3.4% over the year to August. Wages rose 3.0%.
STEP 4: Tariffs are one pressure on prices among many.

CONCLUSION: A tax on imports can come out of your grocery bill. Count both sides before calling it protection.

PREMISE: Payroll taxes, sales taxes and poverty are separate.

STEP 1: Payroll tax hits every dollar of a cashier's pay.
STEP 2: Louisiana's combined sales tax is about 10.1%.
STEP 3: Low-wage families spend nearly everything they earn, so they pay sales tax on nearly everything.
STEP 4: Add the $7.25 floor and the bottom gets squeezed from both sides.

CONCLUSION: Low pay plus regressive taxes is a two-handed squeeze. Fix both.

PREMISE: Big Pharma prices are a health issue, not a wage issue.

STEP 1: Ozempic listed at $969 a month in the U.S. versus $155 in some other countries.
STEP 2: Drug costs feed insurance premiums.
STEP 3: Premiums come out of employer budgets that could go to pay.
STEP 4: Medicare's negotiated prices cut 38% to 79% off the first ten drugs.

CONCLUSION: High drug prices are a hidden pay cut. Negotiation is a raise in disguise.

PREMISE: The Denka case was about one plant, not about jobs or taxes.

STEP 1: EPA sued in 2023 over cancer risk near the LaPlace plant, then dropped the case in 2025.
STEP 2: Denka suspended production in May 2025, blaming compliance costs.
STEP 3: Workers lost shifts. Neighbors were left with uncertainty.
STEP 4: Neither group had a plan for what came next.

CONCLUSION: Pollution fights and job fights are the same fight. A transition plan protects both.

PREMISE: White workers and Black workers have different economic interests.

STEP 1: Both are paid under the same $7.25 floor in Louisiana.
STEP 2: Both lose when union density falls and labor's share shrinks.
STEP 3: Rural white towns and Black neighborhoods both lose hospitals when Medicaid is cut.
STEP 4: Division keeps the floor low for everyone.

CONCLUSION: Same boss, same floor, same cuts. Class solidarity is self-interest.

PREMISE: Hunger data and disaster data are dry bureaucratic numbers.

STEP 1: USDA ended its hunger survey after the 2024 report.
STEP 2: NOAA retired its billion-dollar disaster database.
STEP 3: Those counts let people link storms to costs and cuts to hunger.
STEP 4: Without them, the dots in every other argument get harder to connect.

CONCLUSION: Cutting data cuts the dots. Defend the counts.

PREMISE: Angola's farm line is a prison issue, not a wage issue.

STEP 1: Angola farm line workers can earn 2 to 4 cents an hour after three years unpaid.
STEP 2: Labor that cheap competes with free workers doing similar jobs.
STEP 3: Any worker who can be paid nearly nothing drags down the floor.
STEP 4: Louisiana's floor is already $7.25.

CONCLUSION: Prison wages are labor policy. A floor with a trapdoor isn't a floor.

PREMISE: Housing and health care are separate budgets.

STEP 1: Housing is the biggest cost for most renters.
STEP 2: Families who spend over half their income on rent cut back on medicine and doctor visits.
STEP 3: Untreated problems end in the ER, which costs more.
STEP 4: Evictions add stress and health risks.

CONCLUSION: A stable home is health care. Housing policy is health policy.

PREMISE: Rental price-fixing is a housing issue, not a wage issue.

STEP 1: DOJ settled with RealPage in November 2025 over its rent-setting software. RealPage admitted no wrongdoing.
STEP 2: Software that helps landlords set rents together can push rents up across a market.
STEP 3: Real wages rose about $2 a week in a year.
STEP 4: When rent rises faster than pay, the raise goes to the landlord.

CONCLUSION: Rent and wages are one budget. A rent hike is a pay cut by another name.

PREMISE: The 2025 budget law is about the federal budget, not Louisiana.

STEP 1: About 1.6 million Louisianans are on Medicaid, and new work rules arrive by the end of 2026.
STEP 2: SNAP cuts shift costs to states.
STEP 3: Louisiana's budget then has to cover more with less.
STEP 4: The state already has the highest poverty rate in the country.

CONCLUSION: Washington's math lands on Louisiana's kitchen tables. Count it locally.

PREMISE: Hospital strikes hurt patients, so they're bad for the public.

STEP 1: Health care workers were about 40% of strikers in 2025, many over staffing.
STEP 2: Short staffing means fewer nurses per patient.
STEP 3: Fewer nurses per patient raises the risk of mistakes and missed care.
STEP 4: A strike over staffing is a fight over patient safety.

CONCLUSION: Nurses and patients are on the same side. Safe staffing protects both.

PREMISE: Noncompetes are a contract issue, not a poverty issue.

STEP 1: The FTC dropped its noncompete ban in September 2025.
STEP 2: A noncompete blocks a worker from taking a better job in the same field.
STEP 3: The easiest way to get a raise is often to switch jobs.
STEP 4: Take away that option and pay stays flat, especially in low-wage towns with few employers.

CONCLUSION: Locking workers in locks wages down. Mobility is money.

PREMISE: Each issue needs its own movement.

STEP 1: Taxes decide who funds services.
STEP 2: Services decide who stays out of poverty.
STEP 3: Wages and unions decide who can afford rent, food and care.
STEP 4: Climate decides what all of it costs on the Gulf.

CONCLUSION: Every issue runs through the same question: who pays and who decides. One movement can answer it.
